column4: The section's alternative reading of كَبَدٍ as upright balance meets the same human-creation formula here: أَحْسَنِ تَقْوِيمٍ makes the body's well-proportioned form explicit.
The section's lexicographic reading of كَبَدٍ as upright and balanced creation is stated through Allah's creating, proportioning, and balancing the human.
The section counts the body as crafted parts; رَكَّبَكَ describes Allah composing a person in whatever form He wills.
The section's body begins in the mother's womb; this ayah says people emerge from their mothers' wombs knowing nothing, then names hearing, sight, and hearts as given faculties.
The section cites the dictionary form مُخَلَّقَةٌ for a fully formed morsel; this creation sequence explicitly contrasts a formed and unformed morsel.
The section's dictionary gloss of مُضْغَةٌ مُخَلَّقَةٌ is completed formation; here the morsel is followed by bones clothed with flesh and another creation.
The section follows bodily making through birth and formed limbs; this ayah traces human life from dust and a drop through an infant, maturity, and old age.
The section's womb and bodily-formation scene meets Allah's forming people in wombs as He wills.
The section brings the formed body back to its prenatal beginning; this ayah describes creation within mothers' wombs, form after form in three darknesses.
The section names the body before and after birth; this ayah recalls people as embryos in their mothers' wombs.
The section's bodily inventory includes the origin of a human body; this ayah asks what a person was created from and answers with a gushing fluid, setting up the next ayah.
The section identifies its dictionary form ترائب as the necklace-place on the chest; this ayah places the issuing fluid between the backbone and ترائب.
The section asks what the bestowed body parts are for; this ayah describes the human being fashioned and given hearing, sight, and hearts, then asks for gratitude.
This ayah says Allah originated people and made hearing, sight, and hearts, the faculties that make the section's question about bodily tools concrete.
The section treats eyes and speech organs as given tools; this ayah names hearing, sight, and hearts as Allah's gifts and asks why people give so little thanks.
The section moves from the body made to its use; this ayah describes a human made from a mixed drop and given hearing and sight for a test.
The section asks how the given faculties are used; this ayah pairs guidance to the way with the human's choice to be grateful or ungrateful.
This ayah explicitly says Allah created the human, matching the section's body as a made, assembled thing; its next ayah specifies an outward human faculty.
The section calls لسان the speech organ; this ayah names البيان, articulate expression, as something taught to the human.
The section gives chest as a lexicographic sense of بلد; this ayah's صَدْرِي is a directly bodily image of an opened chest.
Moses asks for his chest to be opened, meeting the section's lexicographic chest reading for بلد and its bodily frame for speech.
The section presents لسان as the organ that speaks; Moses asks for the knot in his tongue to be loosened.
The section joins tongue and utterance as organ and work; Moses asks that others understand his قول, his speech.
Moses describes his chest tightening and his tongue not setting free; the bodily impediment makes the section's chest, tongue, and speech links concrete.
The section links creation to guidance as a sequence; Abraham confesses that the One who created him is the One who guides him.
The section's inward work of the mouth is feeding; Abraham says that his Lord feeds him and gives him drink.
The section calls لسان the speech organ; this ayah describes each messenger speaking in his people's tongue so the message is clear to them.
The section's bodily لسان extends to spoken language here, where the charge of a foreign informant is answered by the clear Arabic tongue of the message.
The section treats the tongue as the organ of speech; this ayah describes the revelation as being on a clear Arabic tongue.
The section says the given organs are tools with consequences; here tongues, hands, and feet testify against their owners.
The section's boast comes from a speaking mouth and a body equipped with limbs; this ayah seals mouths and lets hands and feet speak, reversing which bodily parts give testimony.
The section's body is made of distinct organs; at judgment, hearing, eyes, and skins testify against their owners.
The section lists body parts as made organs; here the skin itself answers that Allah enabled it to speak, extending testimony beyond the human mouth.
The section's man assumes no one sees him; this ayah says people did not hide from their own hearing, eyes, and skins, but thought Allah did not know much of what they did.
The section sets a boastful utterance beside the belief that no one sees the speaker; this ayah says no قول is uttered without a watcher ready beside the speaker.
The section asks how the body's tools are used; this ayah says hearing, sight, and heart will each be questioned about their use.

The section joins the mouth's two works: giving food and speaking well. This ayah commands provision from an inheritance for present kin, orphans, and needy people together with قولًا معروفًا, a recognized good word.
This covenant command joins care for parents, kin, orphans, and the poor to وَقُولُوا لِلنَّاسِ حُسْنًا, speaking well to people, as the section joins bodily speech with care for the vulnerable.
The section's outward mouth can speak well while its inward work gives food; this ayah says a good word and pardon are better than charity followed by injury.
The section joins release of a neck to feeding the vulnerable; this ayah places care for kin, orphans, and the poor alongside giving فِي الرِّقَابِ, faith, patience, and keeping one's word.
The section's ط ع م discussion turns inward mouth-work toward the vulnerable; this ayah says the righteous feed the needy, orphan, and captive.
The section asks what giving food is for; these feeders explain that they seek God's face and want neither repayment nor thanks.
This ayah pairs eating with feeding the contented and the needy from the sacrifice; it gives the section's inward mouth-work a concrete sharing scene.
The section calls for food on a day of hunger; this ayah says the Lord of the House fed Quraysh against hunger and secured them from fear.
The section's ط ع م form puts asking and feeding in relation; here those with provision reject the request to spend and ask, أَنُطْعِمُ, whether they should feed someone Allah could feed.
The section's dictionary form makes feeding a relation between giver and recipient; this ayah names Allah as the One who feeds and is not fed.
The section directs the mouth and body toward an orphan in need; this ayah depicts the contrary bodily act of harshly repulsing the orphan.
The section describes feeding the poor on a hungry day; this ayah condemns not urging others to feed the poor.
The section's body-part inventory leads toward care for the orphan; this ayah challenges the claim to honor by pointing to failure to honor the orphan.
The section's ط ع م link is feeding a needy person; this ayah condemns failing to urge food for the poor.
The section turns a boast over wealth toward feeding others; this ayah names the contrary act of consuming inheritance indiscriminately.
The section's speaker boasts about spending abundant wealth before the call to feed the needy; this ayah names an excessive love of wealth as part of the surrounding moral failure.
The section calls for food to go toward an orphan's mouth; this ayah forbids consuming orphan property together with one's own, the opposite direction of taking and giving.
The section's feeding action is inverted: unjustly consuming an orphan's wealth becomes fire in the consumer's own belly.
The section explicitly sets feeding the hungry poor against the failure to encourage it; this ayah names that failure in the condemned person's conduct.
The section cites feeding the poor and gives this as its contrary outcome: the condemned person has no food except ghislin.
The section's cited 69:36 names ghislin as the only food; this next ayah adds that only the wrongdoers eat it, turning failed care for the poor into a boundary around who receives that food.
The section's action فَكُّ رَقَبَةٍ releases a person; this ayah uses the same neck-for-person expression in requiring the freeing of a believing neck as expiation.
The section joins neck-release to feeding; this oath expiation offers freeing a neck or feeding ten needy people, directly pairing the two acts.
The section's outward speech and release of the neck meet in a legal consequence of a spoken marital formula: before the couple touches, the speaker must free a neck.
This continuation pairs the section's two mouth directions with neck-release: if the person cannot free a neck or fast, the expiation is feeding sixty poor people.
The section explains الميمنة as the side named from the right hand; this ayah repeats the designation أصحاب الميمنة for the people of the right.
This paired ayah names أصحاب المشأمة opposite the right-side party, making the bodily right/left boundary in the section's term visible.
This later passage again calls a saved group أصحاب اليمين, repeating the section's movement from right-hand wording to a group designation.
This ayah repeats أصحاب اليمين as a group label, echoing the section's derivation of الميمنة from the right-hand side.
The section names both birth from the womb and كَبَدٍ as hardship; this ayah makes bodily bearing a form of hardship for the mother.
The section explains the right-side group through the word for the right hand; this judgment scene gives one person his record in his right hand, where the bodily word carries an outcome.
The section links الميمنة to the right hand; this paired judgment scene gives another person his record in the left hand, marking the opposite outcome.
This judgment scene again gives the record to the right hand, making the bodily right-hand image a sign of an outcome, as in the section's right-side designation.
The section's right-side term derives from the hand; this paired scene gives the record from behind the back, an opposite bodily sign to the right hand.
The section derives the right-side designation from the hand; this ayah calls people by their record, with the successful receiving it in the right hand.

The next verse reverses the section's bodily uprightness and the preceding verse's best proportion by returning the human to the lowest state; the expression may mean bodily decline or another lower state, so the bodily reading is uncertain.
The section asks how given organs are used; this ayah pictures people with hearts that do not understand, eyes that do not see, and ears that do not hear, a specific failure of those faculties.
The section's body is equipped with hearing, sight, and hearts; this ayah says those faculties did not avail a people when they rejected the signs.
The section presents freeing a neck; this ayah depicts necks encircled by shackles and chins forced upward, the bodily opposite of release.
The section's neck can be freed; this ayah pictures collars around necks in its account of those who reject resurrection.
The section makes the tongue the organ of speech; this ayah depicts people twisting their tongues while presenting words as scripture, a concrete misuse of the organ.
The section asks what an outward-speaking mouth is used for; this ayah condemns tongues that falsely declare what is lawful and forbidden.
The section treats the tongue as a speech organ; this ayah depicts people passing words from tongue to tongue without knowledge and thinking the matter slight.
